idiom_name: serde custom Serialize/Deserialize + aes-gcm AEAD sealing + zeroize for erasure
implementation_notes: serde is Rust's dominant serialization framework and its Serialize/Deserialize traits are the exact extension point the pattern needs: a hand-written Serialize impl (or #[serde(with = "...")]) writes only the AEAD-sealed bytes of the protected map, sealing with aes-gcm (Aes256Gcm::new(key).encrypt(nonce, plaintext, aad)) or ring's AEAD, and zeroize/Zeroizing wipes plaintext and key buffers on drop. What replaces the classic structure: the Serialize/Deserialize pair plus a newtype around the protected map replaces the class's two maps, and a hand-written Debug impl (never #[derive(Debug)]) replaces the masked-list rendering, because the derive prints every field. This is the rare case where the language ecosystem supplies both the serialization hook and a dependable erasure primitive.
pitfalls: Serde has no reflection over the impl: a field added to the struct but not to the hand-written Serialize/Deserialize is silently dropped from the wire, and a field accidentally added to the impl leaks - test the serialized shape, not just the struct.
AES-GCM nonces must be unique per key and the crate will not stop reuse: generate a random 96-bit nonce per seal (or a guaranteed-unique counter) and store it with the ciphertext.

#[derive(Debug)] - and Clone - will print or copy plaintext; implement Debug by hand, zeroize plaintext immediately after sealing, and remember that String reallocations can leave copies in the allocator that zeroize cannot reach.
Deserialize runs on attacker-controlled bytes: bound the payload length before decrypting, treat an AEAD failure as tampering (never unwrap), and do not let a malformed length panic the process.
